newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian economy does better than forecast.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian economy does better than forecast.

text.p: The Italian economy grew slightly more than expected in the third quarter of 1996, with imports and exports both rising strongly, national statistics office Istat said on Tuesday.
Istat said Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.7 percent year-on-year between July and September and 0.6 percent by comparison with the second quarter.
Provisional data released by Istat last November pointed to a 0.5 percent increase in both cases.

Over the first three quarters of the year, the economy grew by 0.9 percent against the same period in 1995, with the construction, agriculture and service sectors all showing gains while the industry sector declined 0.4 percent.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has forecast growth of 0.8 percent for 1996 as a whole and an Istat spokesman described this goal as realistic on Tuesday.

Early data has pointed to industrial output increasing in both October and November but the final quarter of the year has two fewer working days than the fourth quarter of 1995, which will depress the overall GDP figure.
However, Enrico Giovannini, head of the Istat department which compiles GDP data, said the 1996 target could be hit even with around zero growth in the last three months of the year.

This would come as a relief to the government, which has repeatedly revised its economic forecasts downwards in the face of faltering industrial production, strong lira gains and stringent Bank of Italy monetary policy at the start of 1996.
The original 1996 GDP target was for a repeat of 1995's three percent growth.
The economy actually declined in the second quarter of 1996, while imports fell in three successive quarters and exports remained basically stagnant over four quarters.

However, imports rose 1.1 percent in the third quarter compared with the quarter before, while exports jumped two percent. "This inversion of the trend is typical of an economic recovery," Istat's Giovannini said.

Istat said the climb in exports could be put down to companies cutting margins in a bid to overcome the stronger lira. It also pointed out that despite the gain in imports, private consumption remained weak, increasing just 0.2 percent on a quarterly basis.

This slight rise was thanks largely to more money being spent on semi-durable goods, such as clothing, while for the third quarter in succession spending on durable goods, like cars and domestic appliances, dropped.
In a bid to boost the depressed vehicle market, the government has just announced incentives to encourage people to buy cars.
Car maker Fiat is Italy's largest private company and the vehicle industry is crucial to the country's economy. Any increase in car sales would help GDP.

Prodi's government is sticking to forecasts of growth of two percent this year but most economists say this is optimistic given the 1997 austerity budget, which was approved by parliament last month and includes a number of tax hikes.
Further tough budgetary measures will almost certainly be needed in early 1997 to cover a bigger-than-expected public sector deficit in 1996, due in part to the sluggish economy.
The Italian employers' organisation Confindustria and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have predicted growth of 1.2 percent in 1997.
